rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: PFA: Attention Can Be Progressively Focused in Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Pengjie Zhou, Weiqin Yang, Haibo Xing, Hao Deng, Jinxin Hu
papers.summary: The authors at Alibaba found that when a generative recommender decodes with beam search, attention concentrates on a few past behaviors as decoding proceeds, and which behaviors matter stays largely the same from step to step. Building on this, PFA picks the important history once for the whole decode, instead of having every beam pick it again at every step. It attends to the full history as usual at the first decoding step. At the second step it pools the beams' attention over the history, weighted by generation probability, into one shared ranking of important behaviors, and it shrinks the number of kept behaviors by a fixed ratio at each later step. In an online A/B test on an e-commerce ads platform, the user history grew from 128 to 512 behaviors, revenue rose 3.76%. Response time stayed below that of feeding the full history directly.

papers.title: Towards Reliable, Scalable, and Value-Aligned Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale Advertising
papers.authors: Yatong Xiao, Yibo Sheng, Lixiang Wang, Mingjie Sun, Yunhao Sha, Pengfei Zhang, Shengyu Wang, Peng Wang, Wenjin Wu, Peng ...
papers.summary: Kuaishou made three changes to GR4AD, its deployed generative ad retrieval system, and the result, GR4AD-X, raises online ad revenue by a cumulative 3.07% over GR4AD. All three target the same mismatch: the model picks ads by generation probability, while the platform cares about revenue. The top ten ads by generation probability and the top ten by eCPM barely overlap, with a hit rate of only about 0.02. The first change keeps the two nearest first-level cluster centers for each ad, so it can still be retrieved when one prefix is pruned. The second skips a bigger backbone and instead feeds in twenty-odd extra user-profile and context features from the ranking system and widens the embeddings of key features. The third estimates a revenue value for each SID prefix, namely the mean revenue of the ads beneath it. During pruning, RRF combines each prefix's positions in the probability ranking and in the value ranking into one score, and candidates are cut by that score. ==The changes were stacked one at a time in online tests==.

papers.title: UGR: Unified Generative Ranking for Heterogeneous E-commerce Recommendation
papers.authors: Zonghe Shao, Huabin Chen, Sitong Lu, Fangmei Zhu, Yingcai Ma, Ge Fan, Jinguo Gao, Wei Shi, Yanfang Liu, Huiping Chu
papers.summary: Taobao's generative ranking framework UGR has one generative model directly produce the screen the user finally sees. The roughly one thousand organic, ad and other-business candidates of a request go to the model together, and it generates the final list item by item, instead of each business ranking its own items and a blending stage stitching them together. That stitching step is the old problem: the blender inserts other content into the generator's list, positions and context change, and the order the model learned no longer holds. In an online A/B test on Guess You Like, transaction volume rose 3.29%; when the same model ranks only organic items and hands them to the old blender, transaction volume rises only 2.84%, and ==the gap is the value of unified generation itself==.

papers.title: RoFiGR: Coarse Routing, Fine Refinement via Level-Adaptive Distillation in Multimodal Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Ji Dai, Zhipeng Wei, Zhuang Zhuang, Rongfeng Guo, Jie Chen, Quan Fang, Fei Pan
papers.summary: A generative recommender produces an item's SID one code at a time, and once the first two codes pick the wrong branch, no amount of later precision can recover the relevant items. In multimodal recommendation the SIDs are mostly built from image and text semantics, so their first codes may not reflect which items the same users tend to buy. RoFiGR therefore concentrates collaborative signal on the first two codes. When building the SIDs, it pulls the sum of each item's first two code vectors toward that item's embedding from a frozen sequential recommender (MISSRec), an embedding learned from user behavior. During generation, the same model acts as a teacher: it scores every item, a branch's target probability is the sum of the probabilities of the items under it, and the student learns from these at every step. On three Amazon datasets, it leads in all 15 comparisons across five ranking metrics (HR@10, NDCG@10 and others), and its relative gain over the strongest baseline averages about 9.4% across these 15.

papers.title: R2QRec: Learning Recommendation Queries from Retrieval Feedback
papers.authors: Weixin Chen, Shuchang Liu, Hailan Yang, Yuhan Zhao, Li Kang, Xuefeng Zhang, Chenghao Zhang, Xinyuan Wang, Hanchen Yang, ...
papers.summary: One way to use an LLM for recommendation is to have it write a few search queries from the user's history and pass them to an existing retrieval system. The catch is that logs record what the user clicked, not what query should have been written. The common fix imitates the clicked item's text, but such a query may not actually retrieve that item. R2QRec checks queries with a fixed retriever instead. It first generates many candidate queries and keeps only those that really retrieve the clicked item as SFT targets. The model then writes a set of queries, each retrieves a list, RRF merges the lists into one recommendation list, and GRPO rewards the set by where the clicked item lands in it. Only the query generator is trained; the retriever and item index stay fixed. On MovieTV, removing the retrieval check drops NDCG@10 from 5.07% to 4.03%.

papers.title: Statistical Detection of Positional Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems: Methodologies and Empirical Evidence
papers.authors: Carlos Peláez-González, Francisco Herrera, Andrés Herrera-Poyatos
papers.summary: Put candidate products into a prompt and ask an LLM to recommend one, and the order of the candidates by itself changes the pick. The authors built a RAG recommendation testbed on a real product catalog, shuffled the candidate order repeatedly for each query, and tested 8 models. Statistical tests confirmed that the recommendation depends on position for every model. The direction differs by model: GPT-OSS favors items listed first, while LLaMA 4 Scout avoids the first slot. It gets worse with more candidates. With 20 candidates, merely shuffling the order makes 58.1% of DeepSeek R1 7B's recommendations differ from the product it most often gives for the same query. The bias comes from the model itself and does not go away with a different temperature, so teams using LLMs for recommendation should randomize candidate order and audit for this regularly.

papers.title: Merge and Branch: Efficient Tree-Structured Supervised Fine-Tuning of LLMs for Recommendation
papers.authors: Yunqin Zhu, Yao Xie
papers.summary: In LLM generative recommendation, the input is a long, text-heavy history while the output is an SID of just a few tokens. Training spends a lot of compute reading a whole history and then usually learns only one target item from it. Merge and Branch first squeezes each history item into a handful of tokens. The item's per-level SID embeddings are combined into one anchor vector. A few learned offset vectors are each added to the anchor to form queries, which attend over the item's SID and text tokens. What each query picks up is added back onto the anchor vector to form one token. Second, the compressed history predicts several targets at once: the next item, later items and items a teacher model recommends. The targets share the same history like branches of a tree and cannot see each other. Beams share one history KV cache at decoding time. ==The history is computed once and every branch still sends gradients back==. At a history length of 512, beam search uses 61.8% less memory and runs about a tenth faster.

papers.title: Federated Recommender Agents
papers.authors: Jaehyung Lim, Woojoo Kim, Junyoung Kim, Dongha Kim, Wonbin Kweon, Hwanjo Yu
papers.summary: LLM recommender agents face a choice: pooling every user's memories raises privacy concerns, while isolated agents cannot learn from each other. FedRecAgent lets each client-side agent upload only experiences written in natural language, with no interaction logs and no model parameter updates. Each experience has three parts: what situation the user was in, how the next choice went (staying with the current interest, returning to an earlier one, or trying something new), and why. Specific items and personal preferences are stripped out. The server uses text similarity to group experiences with similar situations, merges those in a group whose choices are also alike, and keeps different choices apart. At recommendation time the next choice is unknown, so each client finds the group closest to its current situation, uses its local memories of preferences and choice habits to shortlist the best-matching experiences in that group, and lets the model pick one to guide ranking. Across six datasets, the best variant beats the strongest baseline on NDCG@10 by 1.54% to 9.19%.

papers.title: PALATE: Pretrained Autoregressive LATent Embeddings
papers.authors: Sizhang Zhao, Praveen Gondhi, Bin Li, Utsaw Kumar
papers.summary: Ads ranking on food-delivery and local-commerce marketplaces needs strong personalization, yet user histories are sparse and there are hundreds of thousands of stores. DoorDash's ranker used to rely on hand-built count features and order-free pooled history, with no learned representation of a user's sequence. PALATE trains a GPT-style model to predict which stores a user will engage with next from their behavior sequence, and takes the hidden state at the last position as the user embedding. It is refreshed daily and fed to the ranker of every ad surface as an ordinary feature. Because repeat orders dominate, training gives more weight to stores new to the user, pretrains on clicks and then fine-tunes on orders. Offline it is the largest single-feature AUC gain. Online it shipped inside bundled ranker retrains, and on search ads revenue rose 0.94% and conversion rate rose 1.50%.

papers.title: Category-Anchored Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation
papers.authors: Lexi Bai, Xiaopeng Zeng, Xun Zhou, Yuanshao Zhu, James Jianqiao Yu
papers.summary: When predicting a user's next point of interest (POI), asking an LLM to generate the POI ID directly is unreliable: POIs are numerous, scattered and long-tailed, and their names carry little meaning. ANCHOR changes the order. The LLM first predicts what category of place the user wants next, which is easier because categories are few and stable. Candidates are then gathered from three sources: places in that category, places the user has visited, and places in the categories the user favors over the long term, recently and at that time of day. Finally a reranker that looks at the user's past trajectories picks the specific place. Guessing the category first and then the place is steadier than guessing the place outright. On check-in datasets from New York, Tokyo and California, ANCHOR beats the strongest LLM baseline, Think2Go, on Acc@1 by 7.56%, 11.21% and 1.94%.

papers.title: Beyond IPS: Reliable Counterfactual Evaluation in Multi-Stage Ad Systems without Logged Propensities
papers.authors: Mohsen Malmir, Mohamed A. Radwan, Houssam Nassif, Murat Ali Bayir
papers.summary: Before an ad system launches a new ranking model, it must pick the best candidate offline from logs. In multi-stage delivery, impressions pass through auctions, filters and caching, and their selection probabilities are never logged, so IPS cannot be used. The usual substitute scores new policies with a click-predicting reward model, but new policies push impressions toward ads that are rare in the logs, where that model is least accurate. The authors replay the candidates on past requests and train a classifier to tell whether an impression comes from the logs or from a given candidate. For each logged impression, the classifier gives the ratio of its probability under each candidate to its probability under the logs. The average of these ratios over all candidates becomes its weight when training one shared reward model, so impressions that look like what the candidates would show count more. Five candidates in a production CTR ranking system all ran in A/B tests. Picking a winner on each of 50 random log subsamples, the rate of picking the truly best one rises from 0.36 without weighting to 0.40.

papers.title: PRISM: Personalized Item Representations in User History
papers.authors: Renzhi Wu, Zikun Cui, Junjie Yang, Li Sheng, Yongjun Xie, Jerry Fu, Nipun Mathur, Sri Reddy, Hong Li
papers.summary: The same cooking video is a pastime for a casual viewer and source material for a food creator. Yet a recommender gives it the same starting embedding in both users' history sequences. PRISM replaces each history event with a new vector. That vector expresses how this user related to this item at that moment. It reuses the intermediate states of every layer that the upstream ranking model already computed while scoring, and an autoencoder compresses them into one embedding per scored user–item pair. These are stored, and later sequence models read them in time order. On a billion-scale recommendation surface at Meta, downstream NE drops by 0.15% on average. At a similar history length, VISTA, another approach that caches history summaries, drops by only 0.07%. The gain also grows with longer histories. ==The input to a history sequence can itself be personalized==.

papers.title: Read More, Reason Deeper: Latent Workspaces for Long-Sequence Recommendation
papers.authors: Renzhi Wu, Li Sheng, Zikun Cui, Junjie Yang, Tai Guo, Keke Zhai, Yan Li, Jerry Fu, Nipun Mathur, Sri Reddy, Hong Li
papers.summary: This Meta paper gives long-sequence ranking a new structure in which reading more history and stacking more layers become two separately tunable knobs: with 10K history events, its NE beats HSTU by 0.19% while using 69.6% less forward compute. Current models tie the two together. A sequence encoder pays for every extra event in every layer, while models that first select relevant events select only once, so later layers never see what was left out. LWR gives each candidate a small fixed set of vectors as a workspace: some are generated from its features, and some are learned vectors shared by all candidates. Every layer forms queries from the workspace, reads the full history with weights, and uses what it reads to update the workspace for the next layer. ==Reading more and stacking deeper can be scaled separately==.

papers.title: Floor It, Then Fill It: Simulating Creator Ecosystems for Fair Video-Content Recommendation Systems at Billion User Scale
papers.authors: Sohini Roychowdhury, Long Sha, Sunand Agarwal, Payal Kamboj, Shuyang Chen, Junlin Zhang, Scott Chen, Hui Zhang
papers.summary: Recommenders allocate traffic by engagement, so big creators keep growing and newcomers struggle to be seen. Testing traffic policies that support newcomers directly in production is costly, so the authors build a simulator of about 42K creators whose makeup and overall metrics are calibrated to the real platform, and compare traffic allocation methods inside it. The best one gives creators a weekly guaranteed view target, and the allocation algorithm uses how far a creator still falls short of it as its reward, so the small creators furthest behind get supported traffic first. With it, 90% of the guaranteed targets are met each week, and small creators' organic reach grows by about 33% per week. The authors also discuss when fairness conclusions drawn from a simulator can be trusted.

papers.title: Revisiting Temporal Link Prediction through Structural Proximity
papers.authors: Yuzhang Fei, Yanping Zheng, Lu Yi, Zhewei Wei
papers.summary: Temporal link prediction guesses who will interact with whom next. Recent methods mostly learn ever more complex temporal representations, yet a classical method can match or beat them. The authors run Personalized PageRank directly on the historical interaction graph, adding only a sliding window or a time decay that shrinks the weight of old edges, with no training at all. Across 14 datasets, the time-decay version ranks first on 9 and second on 4, even on datasets with few repeated edges. The reason is that paths in the history graph leading to new destinations already carry a strong signal. ==Current benchmarks may overstate the value of complex temporal models==, and new methods should be compared against classical baselines like this one.

papers.title: CASH: A Capability-Aware Subsidy Harness for Advertiser Subsidy Allocation
papers.authors: Minmao Wang, Huihuang Lin, Likang Wu, Hongke Zhao, Shijie Yi, Fei Pan
papers.summary: Ad platforms give advertisers billing discounts, usually set by operators through tier-based rules. Those rules cannot capture how each account responds to different discount levels. CASH needs to predict how much revenue each account brings at each discount level, and it does so in two ways at once: an LLM that carries business knowledge, and a numerical model learned from historical data. It measures each one's errors on accounts whose outcomes are already known, for each kind of account and discount level, and only a side whose error is small enough is licensed to predict for that level. Each account then uses one side's predictions and only that side's licensed levels. When both sides have licensed levels, a scorer trained on which side erred less in the past picks one; when neither does, the account gets no discount. The system then picks every account's discount level together under the total budget to maximize total revenue. In a one-month online experiment covering 60% of the platform's traffic, with the subsidy rate essentially unchanged, the platform's revenue per account rises by 15.35%, and longer-term metrics such as retention improve as well.

papers.title: Bridging Semantics and Structure: A Theoretically Grounded Framework for Link Prediction on TAGs
papers.authors: Chen Shao, Ruirui Wang, Tobias Kafer, Danai Koutra
papers.summary: Link prediction on text-attributed graphs, such as predicting whether two papers will cite each other, is usually done by combining a language model with a GNN, but how best to fuse the two is still unsettled. Bridge-LP takes a simple route. It lets the language model's text embeddings bypass the GNN layers and join the final node embeddings used for scoring, so the loss gradient flows straight back to the language model and training is more stable. And during training it re-encodes text only for the nodes in the current batch of edges, using cached embeddings for all other nodes, which saves a lot of compute. Compared with 40 existing models on 9 datasets, it beats the strongest baseline on Cora by 43.06% in MRR. Neither design is expensive, so teams working on graph-based recommendation can try each one separately.

papers.title: DeepCommerceRec: a graph- and sequence-aware deep learning recommender system with cold-start adaptation for large-scale e-commerce platforms
papers.authors: Kumbham Bhargavi, Soanpet Sree Lakshmi, B. Sreenivasu, M. Shanthi, Kiran Kumar Reddy Penubaka, B. Nagadivya
papers.summary: E-commerce recommendation has to handle three things at once: long-term collaborative preferences, short-term purchase intent, and new users and items with almost no interactions. DeepCommerceRec learns them with two encoders. One learns structural user-item relations on a heterogeneous graph, and the other learns how interests change over time from behavior sequences. A small MLP reads both vectors plus signals such as interaction count and cold-start flags, and outputs a weight between 0 and 1 for each dimension to mix the two. For a new user, the sequence representation is replaced by a weighted combination of their few most recent items, with more recent ones weighted higher. On three public datasets, Amazon, YooChoose and RetailRocket, the authors report better HR@10, NDCG@10 and MRR than a range of baselines. The method mostly combines existing parts, and the most useful idea for real systems is adjusting the fusion weights by how cold a user or item is.

papers.title: Hidden Disparities in Ranking: Category-Aware Fairness via Distributional Stability
papers.authors: Gayane Taturyan, Charlotte Laclau, Stephan Clémençon
papers.summary: A common fairness check for rankings asks whether different user groups get the same average utility, but this can hide problems. The authors simulate a job platform where the historical data miss women's interest in managerial jobs and men's interest in administrative jobs. Women are then under-served on managerial jobs and men on administrative ones, yet the two gaps cancel out and the overall gap stays near zero. The authors therefore require equal utility across groups within each job category. They prove this is equivalent to the average utility in each category staying the same when only the share of each group changes and each group's own makeup stays fixed. They then search mixtures of existing ranking policies for the one with the highest utility that meets the constraint, validating it on MovieLens-1M. ==Looking only at overall fairness metrics can miss bias inside categories==.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.authors: Raphael Kim, Michele Santacatterina, Ramin Zabih, Keith Barnatchez
papers.summary: Variables visible in training logs are not always usable at deployment. A clinical decision tool, for example, may be trained with patients' socioeconomic information but barred from using it as an input when deployed, to prevent discrimination. The authors call this case, complete logs but restricted deployment, runtime confounding. In reinforcement learning it is harder, because earlier decisions shape later states and actions, so the bias accumulates over time. Their approach estimates the logging policy's action probabilities and a return model with all variables, while the new policy sees only deployment-time variables. The new policy's probability of the logged action divided by the logging policy's reweights the logs, and the return model corrects the result. Both policy learning and off-policy evaluation build on this estimate, and the evaluation gives valid confidence intervals. They also give a test that measures how much return is lost by not being allowed to use those variables. Features that recommendation and ad systems log but cannot use online for privacy or compliance reasons pose the same kind of problem.

papers.title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
papers.authors: Sedigheh Eslami, Markus Krimmel, William Barber, Antoine Chaffin, Maximilian Schall, Jonas Golde, Louis Milliken, Ekater...
papers.summary: Contextual embeddings are trained and evaluated as if a question had only one relevant chunk in a document, and this paper shows that assumption fails in RAG. Answering a question often also needs the chunks that say which product or which year the answer is about, yet current training treats every chunk of the same document other than the answer chunk as a negative, so these supporting chunks get pushed down. The authors use an existing context compression model as the teacher. Its normal job is to pick out the parts of a retrieved document relevant to the query, and it gives every token a relevance score. Each chunk's score is the mean of its top few token scores, and the embedding model learns to match it, so no answer-chunk labels are needed. On a new diagnostic benchmark, the 9B model finds the answer in its top 10 chunks for 45.5% of queries, against 31.1% for the strongest baseline, voyage-context-4.

papers.title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
papers.authors: Dingyi Kang, Bingzhe Li
papers.summary: The work that multi-hop question answering piles onto one LLM can be split up. In this paper's DeFT-RAG, the LLM writes one sub-question at a time that names every entity it asks about. A program records each sub-question and its answer in a QA table by fixed rules, and the LLM reads this table at the end to answer the original question. On MuSiQue, accuracy rises from the strongest baseline's 0.577 to 0.629. Because each sub-question names its entities in full, answers can also be reused across questions: 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache and LLM calls drop by 12.9%, with no loss in accuracy. Multi-hop questions are hard because evidence must be found link by link through intermediate entities the question never names. Iterative methods make the LLM plan, order, rewrite and keep track at once, and each task fails in its own way.

papers.title: Decompose, Estimate, Select: Coverage-Aware Context Construction for Long-Form RAG
papers.authors: He Tu, Aleena Bosco Kurumthottam, Torsten Suel
papers.summary: In long-form RAG, more complete retrieval does not necessarily mean a more complete answer. The paper shows this with a retrieval pipeline it builds that computes coverage explicitly. The authors have an LLM split the question into a set of sub-questions, use a cross-encoder to predict which sub-questions each candidate document can answer, and then repeatedly pick the document that answers the most sub-questions not yet covered. On TREC RAG 2024, α-nDCG rises from 0.625 to 0.702, close to the ceiling reached when human-written answer nuggets replace the sub-questions. Yet in a controlled comparison with the generator, candidate pool and document budget fixed, documents chosen directly with the reference labels cover more, but put no more nuggets into the answer. ==Answer completeness depends not only on what is retrieved but also on whether the generator uses it.==

papers.title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
papers.authors: Adilet Metinov, Chingiz Arziev
papers.summary: RAG systems usually serve a reranker and a generator side by side, and the candidate passages are read once by each model. Glance starts from the idea that the generator reads these passages anyway, so it may as well rank them. It prefills all candidate passages into the KV cache once and attaches a short scoring prompt for each passage on top of that shared cache. A small set of LoRA weights and a scoring head turn each prompt into a relevance score. Then the LoRA is switched off, and the same model reads the selected passages and writes the answer. Each extra decision skill costs about 0.1 GiB of memory. After brief fine-tuning on MS MARCO, it reaches nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact, against 0.721 for the dedicated reranker bge-reranker-v2-m3. The evaluation covers only two retrieval datasets and one model family, but serving one fewer resident model has a direct effect on serving cost.

papers.title: Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Chenjie Qiu, Zixuan Zeng, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Dongsheng Luo, Boyan Xu
papers.summary: Chain embedding retrievers for multi-hop retrieval see different histories in training and in use, and this paper fixes that without adding any LLM call. At each step such a retriever joins the question with the passages found so far to look for the next one; in training its history holds only correct passages, but in use it often holds wrong passages it found itself. On four-hop MuSiQue questions, 70% of the retrieval states already contain a wrong passage by the third step. The authors let the current model run on the training questions every epoch and train it on the states it actually reaches, with the earliest still-missing correct passage as the target. With the same recipe, the share of questions whose full evidence is in the top five rises from 44.6% to 50.5%.

papers.title: xPRT: Cross-Passage Retrieval Pretraining
papers.authors: Danush Khanna, Himanshu Singhal, Pranjal A. Chitale, Bishal Santra
papers.summary: Which passages of the same web page talk about related things is, by itself, enough to train a retriever. xPRT first takes passages whose vectors are close enough to the page's mean vector as anchor passages, then, by vector similarity and word overlap, finds for each anchor the four most related passages of the same document. It then trains the embedding: the anchor must pick out its most related passage from candidates mixed with passages of other documents. Once most words of a related passage are masked, a one-layer decoder must use the anchor's vector to fill them back in. Continuing pre-training from the already strong E5 with only the objective changed, five established objectives gain at most 0.38 points on MTEB, while xPRT gains about 1.8 points consistently. ==What matters most is how positives are chosen; the new fill-in term adds only a small part.==

papers.title: How Specific Do I Need to Be? Effects of User Query Underspecification on Deep Research Agents
papers.authors: Yi Wen, Xiangjue Dong, Bingxuan Li, Hangxiao Zhu, Leo Zhicheng Liu, Yu Zhang, James Caverlee
papers.summary: When users ask a deep research agent a question, they often leave out the time range, use the wrong technical term, or skip their preferences. The authors remove or blur each kind of information in fully specified questions and compare the answers of three deep research agents. Without the scope or the terminology, the answers cover the user's real need much less well, yet citations stay accurate and there is no more hallucination. The search traces suggest why: with a vague question the agent searches more broadly, and fewer of its search terms come from the user's words while more come from what the model learned in training. Agents trained specifically for deep research, which score higher on complete questions, lose more. ==Deep research agents need to learn to ask first when a question is unclear, instead of guessing.==

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Pairwise Ranking Aggregation via Active LLM Feedback
papers.authors: Quan Mai, Susan Gauch, Gibson Nkhata
papers.summary: When fusing results from several retrievers, unsupervised methods such as RRF are cheap but do not learn, while listwise LLM reranking works well but needs hundreds of calls per query. LLM-IRA takes a middle path. It picks only document pairs that the retrievers order in opposite ways (BM25 prefers A over B while dense retrieval prefers B over A) and asks an LLM which one is more relevant. These judgments are used to learn the fusion weights of the retrievers, so the final ranking is still a simple weighted sum of scores. With an open 8B instruction model as the judge, it matches or beats the best static fusion on most benchmarks; on two years of TREC DL it already passes the best unsupervised fusion with about 5 LLM calls per query. It needs no training data and no fine-tuning, which suits settings that want to spend only a small LLM budget at the fusion step.

papers.title: Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration for Spectral Compression of Dense Retrieval Embeddings
papers.authors: Yongkang Li, Panagiotis Eustratiadis, Evangelos Kanoulas
papers.summary: Projecting retrieval embeddings onto a few principal directions is a common way to cut storage and scoring cost, but how much weight each direction keeps follows only an overall trend from corpus statistics, not how much that direction helps separate relevant from irrelevant documents. RRC uses relevance labels to re-estimate each direction's weight: the larger and steadier a direction's contribution to the score gap between relevant and irrelevant documents, the higher its weight. It then fits a power-law curve to the overall trend of these weights and adds only each direction's departure from that curve to the existing weights, so the original trend of high weights on strong directions and low weights on weak ones stays. It only changes the linear transform shared by queries and documents, with no model training and no extra inference step. On five datasets of the reasoning-heavy BRIGHT benchmark, compressed to 768 dimensions, nDCG@10 is on average 2.34 points higher than the original compressor SpecTemp, and the gain holds after quantization.

papers.title: Feedback-Assisted Trust Propagation over Document Relation Graphs for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Zhuoheng Li, Ying Chen
papers.summary: RAG corpora often contain outdated, contradictory or unreliable documents, and labeling which ones are trustworthy by hand is expensive, so labels cover only a small part. This paper treats each document as a node in a graph. Two documents from the same source, or that support each other, get a support edge, and two that contradict each other get a contradiction edge. These relations can be judged by an NLI model. Humans mark only a few documents as reliable or not. It then solves an optimization problem. The trust scores at the two ends of a support edge should be close. The two scores across a contradiction edge should add up to about 1, so at most one is trusted. The scores should also fit the human feedback. That is how trust spreads from the few labeled documents to the whole corpus. Both retrieval and answer generation use the score. The authors report better retrieval quality and EM than the baselines, and stable results when feedback is sparse or noisy.

papers.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Abhishek Malvankar, Paul Castro, Nick Mitchell, Lionel Villard
papers.summary: The table in vLLM's documentation that sets how many tokens speculative decoding guesses per step at each batch size can visibly cut throughput on a different GPU or model. This paper gives a tool that measures the best table in minutes and keeps correcting it as traffic changes. Speculation only pays while the GPU has spare compute, so the more requests share a batch, the fewer tokens each step should guess. TableTune times every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and picks the highest-throughput table. Once in production, a plugin reads vLLM's counts of accepted guesses, combines them with the measured step times, and rewrites the table with the length that yields the most useful tokens per second at each batch size. On a mixture-of-experts model, against the fastest fixed draft length at each load, the documented table is up to 18% slower and the measured table at most 3% slower.

papers.title: FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving
papers.authors: Xin Huang, Teng Ma, Zhuoran Li, Yibo Zhao, Zhaoshi Li, Qianchao Zhu, Wei Yang, Chenxi Wang, Tao Xie, Youwei Zhuo
papers.summary: After analyzing eight production LLM request traces, the authors find that the common practice of treating host memory as a KV cache layer in front of the SSD barely filters any reads under these workloads. Reused blocks either come back only after a long gap, or belong to agent sessions of several gigabytes each that memory cannot hold, so the SSD always ends up on the read path. FlatCake puts memory and SSD at the same level and decides each block's home when it is created. Shared system prompts and short-reply chats go to memory, while multi-gigabyte agent sessions are written straight to the SSD. A session's blocks are stored contiguously and never move, and reads stream large chunks from the SSD straight into the GPU. Replaying a production Claude Code trace, the share of prefixes it reads back instead of recomputing holds at 94% as load rises, while Mooncake drops to 64%. KV storage for long agent sessions should be planned per session.

papers.title: ConfluxServe: Reconciling Resource Utilization and Parallelism Efficiency across Prefill and Decode in LLM Serving
papers.authors: Wenhao Chen, Hong Zhang
papers.summary: In LLM serving, running prefill and decode together lets their resource needs complement each other, since prefill uses compute and decode uses memory bandwidth. But the two want different parallelism. A long-prompt prefill must spread across more GPUs to deliver the first token on time, while decode needs only a few. ConfluxServe treats each operator differently. In the linear layers, tokens from both phases form one batch and are computed together under the same weight sharding. At the attention layers they split: decode stays on its own group of GPUs, while prefill spreads across more GPUs through two All-to-All exchanges. Both paths run at the same time and merge back into one batch afterwards. On production workloads, the request rate it sustains within latency targets is 1.26 to 1.62 times that of the strongest baselines.

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
papers.authors: NVIDIA, Aastha Jhunjhunwala, Aayushi Ashokkumar Srivastava, Abhibha Gupta, Abhinav Garg, Abhinav Khattar, Achsah Wildish...
papers.summary: Open models built for agents often have to choose between capability and inference cost. NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super optimizes both. It is a hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model that activates only about a tenth of its parameters per token, and it scores 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, ahead of the previous-generation Ultra with several times more active parameters. The deployment design matters more to people who serve models. The model carries its own multi-token prediction head for speculative decoding, and post-training trains that head again, raising the average number of accepted tokens per step by up to 21.8% over the untrained head. With NVFP4 quantization, throughput on an interactive agent workload is 2.43 times that of BF16. Base, post-trained and quantized weights are released together with the training data.

papers.title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading
papers.authors: Zhiyuan Fang, Dingyang Li, Jianfeng Zhong, Bin Wang, Weixi Zhu, Cunshu Ni, Zicong Hong, Wuhui Chen, Zibin Zheng
papers.summary: To run a large MoE model on a machine with limited GPU memory, the usual approach keeps some expert weights in host memory and moves them onto the GPU when needed. Even so, GPU memory is still split into two fixed regions, one for experts and one for the KV cache. Under heavy load the KV cache runs short and concurrency stalls. Under light load the KV cache region sits idle but cannot hold extra experts, so expert weights keep being moved back and forth. Rimuru puts both into one shared page pool and adjusts it with load. When requests pile up, more experts leave GPU memory to make room for the KV cache, and when traffic drops, experts move back. To make this work, each kind of data manages the same pool with its own page size, and a rewritten MoE kernel reads expert weights that are not stored contiguously. On two consumer GPUs under heavy load, throughput reaches up to 19.03 times that of KTransformers.

papers.title: SGLang security update: improving request isolation
papers.authors: SGLang Team
papers.summary: In one of Cloudflare's production model deployments, a request received content from another user's session. The SGLang team traced it to the path where prefill and decode run on separate workers. A request that exceeded the prefill KV cache capacity should have been rejected, yet it still went through the handoff, and decode read cache pages that had never been filled for it. They also fixed a related hazard. When a request is interrupted midway, RDMA writes already sent are still in flight, but decode had already returned the destination slots to the allocator, so the late data could land in another request's KV cache without any error. The fix releases the slots only after those writes are confirmed to have landed. On two H100 GPUs, throughput before and after the fix differs by less than 2%. Teams running disaggregated serving should upgrade and check that context length matches cache pool capacity.

papers.title: The Endgame of FSDP Communication: Layout-Aware Collectives on Copy Engines, RDMA, and NVSwitch
papers.authors: Zejian Wang, Yifan Zhao, Kaihui Ren, Xiaoling Zhou, Yubin Wang, Chenhao Guan, Lin Zhang, Yufeng Li, Zhikang Mo, Zhuoru M...
papers.summary: The Kling team's TIDE builds the layout conversion that FSDP2 performs every step directly into communication. Stock FSDP2 stores parameters and gradients one tensor per parameter, but NCCL only sends and receives one flat buffer ordered by GPU, so every step copies data back and forth. TIDE has communication read from where each parameter lives and write straight to where it must end up, with copy engines, RDMA and NVSwitch moving the data and no change to model code or compute kernels. Across three models, step time drops by up to 27.1% relative to stock FSDP2. ==Beyond raw communication speed, data layout and contention for compute decide training speed as well==.

papers.title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
papers.authors: Mads Toftrup, Marco Federici, Boris van Breugel, Paul Whatmough, Markus Nagel
papers.summary: Post-training quantization has to settle three things: each layer's value range, what transform to apply to weights and activations before quantizing, and which way to round each weight. Most methods handle one of these at a time, each minimizing the error at that layer's output, but a small error at one layer does not mean the model's final output changes little. The authors find that a layer's error barely predicts the final impact. It does once the error is weighted by sensitivity, an estimate of how much the model's final output changes when that layer's output shifts slightly in each direction. They then use an approximate Hessian to optimize all three under one objective: how much quantization changes the model's final output. With weights, activations and the KV cache all at 4 bits, it gets the lowest perplexity on all four models, and on the smallest model it lowers perplexity from the best baseline's 17.23 to 16.05.

papers.title: DualQuant: Dual-scale Calibration-free Weight-and-Activation Quantization for LLMs
papers.authors: Mahsa Salmani, Sayeh Sharify, Hesham Mostafa
papers.summary: To get the full speedup of new GPUs with native low-bit math, both weights and activations must be quantized to 4 bits. A few activation channels carry very large values, and the usual fix collects calibration data first and then scales those channels down. DualQuant shows this works without calibration data. It looks only at the weights. To make the quantized weights reconstruct the original weights as closely as possible, it solves for a scaling factor per input channel and multiplies that weight column by it. The same activation channel is then divided by the same factor, which leaves the matrix product unchanged, so these factors end up scaling the activations as well. It supports many formats, including INT4, MX and NVFP4, and on most models and formats it matches or beats the accuracy of SmoothQuant, which needs calibration data. Running real packed 4-bit inference on an RTX 4090, throughput reaches up to 2.46 times that of BF16.

papers.title: DWISE: Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine
papers.authors: Lie Li, Wen Li, Junxiao Shen, Jindong Gu, Guosheng Hu
papers.summary: Diffusion language models denoise many tokens in parallel each round and promise much faster generation than producing one token at a time, but serving frameworks copy the scheduling of autoregressive models: first come, first served, and prefill first. The authors find both rules fit poorly. How many denoising rounds a request needs varies widely and is unknown at arrival, so first come, first served leaves short requests waiting behind long ones. Rounds that run only prompts leave most of the batch idle. These models generate in fixed-size blocks of tokens, and a prompt step and a denoising step each process one block at the same cost. DWISE therefore counts remaining work for both prefill and denoising in block rounds, runs requests with the least left first, and lets both phases share a round. Remaining rounds are first estimated by a small regression model from the prompt's word, line and token counts. After the first denoising round, the model's final-layer hidden states are averaged and passed to a two-layer network that re-estimates them once. Across five models on SGLang, stock SGLang's mean end-to-end latency is 5.4 times that of DWISE.

papers.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
papers.authors: Govind Velamoor, Adrian Lin, Sam Jung, Spencer Mateega, Brandon Y. Yang, Amish Sethi
papers.summary: Most of the training data came from handheld grippers, collected at a different place and under different lighting than the test scene, with only a small share of real-robot teleoperation. Fine-tuned on this mix, pi0.5 succeeded in all 10 trials of a bimanual task that puts oranges into a bowl. The demonstrations come from UMI-Live, an open-source bimanual handheld data-collection system released with the paper. The camera, LiDAR, compute and battery are packed into the gripper, the operator presses one button to record the next take, and a background pipeline turns finished takes into training-ready data. ==UMI-Live's value is not a new algorithm but a data-collection pipeline you can actually reproduce==, and the authors also release about 40 hours of data.

papers.title: FORGE: Feasible Online Reduced-Order Reference Generation and Whole-Body Execution for Agile Humanoid Locomotion
papers.authors: Adrian B. Ghansah, Yujin An, Jeeseop Kim, Soon-Jo Chung
papers.summary: Getting a humanoid to sprint, walk backwards, sidestep, spin in place and hop on one leg usually means preparing reference trajectories or training a separate policy for each behaviour. FORGE does it in two stages. First it trains a reference generator on a simplified body model: forces are computed as if the whole body were one rigid body, while joint poses follow the full robot, and it produces whole-body reference motions in real time from velocity commands. Then it freezes the generator and trains a second policy to track those references on the full robot dynamics. On a Unitree G1, one generator plus one tracking policy covers forward speed of 2.8 metres per second, backward speed of 2 metres per second, one-legged hopping, and smooth switching between these commands. Because the simplified model is cheap to compute, references can be generated online over a wide range of commands.

papers.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere
papers.summary: For a task like the Tower of Hanoi, where a robot must chain many moves, planning with a visual world model tends to drift further off the longer it plans. VQ-WM compresses images into a finite set of discrete states, searches for the shortest path to the goal over those states, then has a controller with visual feedback walk the path segment by segment. The key is how the discrete states are chosen. Instead of clustering by embedding distance, it runs the controller inside the learned world model, and records how many calls it takes to get from each state to a candidate state. It then picks as few candidates as possible so that every state in the data can reach one of them within a few calls. That way every step on the path is within the controller's reach. Trained only on short play data, it reaches 100% task progress on the physical Tower of Hanoi, while existing foundation models such as VLAs succeed only when the full solution happens to be in their training data.

papers.title: Catch It All!: Generalizable Dynamic Catching with a Dexterous Hand
papers.authors: Arth Shukla, Kehlani Fay, Huaze Liu, Darin Djapri, Alexiy Buynitsky, Nicklas Hansen
papers.summary: Catching thrown objects is hard for a humanoid because objects differ so much: plush toys barely bounce, chip bags deform, hard balls rebound on contact, and a humanoid's wrist torque is small enough that overly aggressive motions can damage the hardware. The authors train a reinforcement learning policy only in simulation on simple shapes. Its grasp reward is based on the distance from the fingertips to the object surface, so the closer the fingers wrap the object the higher the reward. A penalty on exceeding rated torque grows over training, so the policy learns to stay within limits. They then deploy it on a Unitree G1 with no real-robot data, using a single camera from the robot's own viewpoint. On objects never seen in training, underhand catches, palm up and low, succeed 38.9% of the time, and overhand catches, hand raised high, succeed 36.1%, while an expert teleoperator manages only 6.8% on the same task. Motions this fast cannot be captured well by teleoperation, so reinforcement learning in simulation is the more realistic route.

papers.title: METATRON: A Promptable Whole-Body Execution Layer for Humanoids
papers.authors: Chen Tessler, Yifeng Jiang, Alec Otto, Yi Shi, Umar Iqbal, Gal Chechik, Xue Bin Peng
papers.summary: Walking, recovering from a shove, picking things up and sitting down usually each need their own trained humanoid controller, even though all of them rely on the same balance and whole-body coordination. Metatron separates the two. It first trains one general whole-body policy and freezes it. The policy takes only partial goals, such as where a hand should be at a given moment, how fast to walk, or which style to move in. Each task is written as ordinary code that sends such goals to the policy at every control step, and the policy fills them in as coordinated whole-body motion. Coding agents can tune this task code from motion data without retraining the policy. On a real Unitree G1, one frozen model handles walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup and sitting on furniture. When shoved during walking, two reference-tracking pipelines fail every time once the push exceeds 600 newtons, while Metatron stays upright in 75% of trials at even larger pushes.

papers.title: ProWorld: Multi-View World Model with Proprioceptive Feedback for Closed-Loop Policy Evaluation
papers.authors: Zijun Wang, Tianyi Yan, Haokun Lin, Panwen Hu, Bohang He, Siyu Ren, Xiaoyu Guo, Weijia Liufu, Shuoshuo Xue, Fengjiao Che...
papers.summary: Evaluating robot policies by running trial after trial on a real robot is slow and expensive, so people want to use frames generated by a world model as the test environment. There are two difficulties. The policy needs more than one image for its next step: it needs several camera views and the robot's own joint state. Generative models also tend to draw a missed grasp as a successful lift, making the policy look stronger than it is. ProWorld predicts multi-view video and robot state together and feeds both back to the policy under test. Its training also adds failed manipulations collected in a high-fidelity simulator to suppress that inflation. Across 3 policies and 4 manipulation tasks, the Pearson correlation between its success rates and real-robot success rates reaches 0.95, which suggests its ranking of policies can largely stand in for real-robot trials.

papers.title: Cross-Controller Transfer via In-Context Behavior Adaptation
papers.authors: Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, Dorsa Sadigh
papers.summary: The same action command makes a robot move differently under different controllers: whether it controls joints or the end-effector, whether it sends positions or velocities, and whether stiffness is set high or low all change what the same numbers mean. Pool such data to train one policy and these meanings clash. The authors first show the policy a short interaction record of commands sent and how the robot actually moved afterwards. A Transformer summarises this record into features of the current controller, and the policy adjusts its actions accordingly. In real-robot experiments this raises average success by 33 percentage points over simply pooling the data. On contact-heavy tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, the policy changes its whole strategy with the controller, not just the size of its motions.

papers.title: LocoManiLab: A Unified Testbed for Data, Policies, Controllers, and Deployment in Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Dewei Wang, Jinrui Han, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Xianbo Lu, Jiabao Wu, Jiqin Feng, Jipeng Kong, Xinzhe Liu, Ping Luo, ...
papers.summary: Research on humanoids that walk and manipulate at the same time is hard to compare, because every group uses different policies, controllers and tasks. LocoManiLab puts data collection, training, evaluation and real-robot deployment into one testbed: 234 tasks across five kinds of household scenes, with demonstrations collected by teleoperation in simulation, and twelve policies evaluated under the same controller. On unseen tasks and scenes, success rates generally fall, dropping further as visual perturbations grow, and policies differ clearly in how well they generalise. The authors also recreate 3 real-robot tasks in simulation, and simulation and the real robot rank the policies similarly, so the authors argue policies can be compared in simulation first and then taken to the real robot.

papers.title: JEDI: Joint-Embedding Demonstration Compression for In-Context Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Jiazhao Liang, Zhewen He, Shuaihang Yuan, Hao Huang, Yi Fang
papers.summary: Getting a robot to do a new task from a few demonstrations without updating weights is limited above all by context length. One demonstration spans hundreds of steps of multi-view frames and still takes thousands of tokens after subsampling, so current methods usually fit only one or two. JEDI compresses each demonstration into a few vectors. Rather than training them to reconstruct the demonstrated actions, it trains them to predict the next-stage keyframe of the current episode. During training it also uses demonstrations of a different task or a different step order as negatives, forcing the vectors to keep execution details. In a test where two demonstrations differ only in the order objects are placed, JEDI follows the demonstrated order 84.1% of the time, while a version that compresses only actions manages 52.2%, roughly a coin flip. What a compressed demonstration should keep is the information that predicts what to do next.

papers.title: AgiBot Innovation Day 2026: Full-Stack Releases for Real-World Embodied Deployment
papers.summary: At this year's Innovation Day, AgiBot proposed a new unit, Worken (effective intelligent work hours), meant to answer how much useful work robots actually do. AgiBot's analogy: steam engines were measured in horsepower, electricity in kilowatt-hours, large models in tokens, and robots should be measured by the hours of valuable work they complete on their own and without interruption, not just by how many are built. At the same event AgiBot released its next-generation embodied foundation model GO-3 Preview, which it says ranks first on three embodied benchmarks and plans to open-source by year end. It also showed an open-source embodied operating system, Lingqu OS, a subcutaneous liquid-cooling system for joints, and a new family of dexterous hands. The industry's focus is shifting from units shipped to how much work robots can do by themselves.
